correctness.rationale: A rank-r map is exactly determined by its rank−1 consecutive fiber cuts and increasing image, giving the stated class size. Idempotents select one fixed image point per fiber, giving the coefficient of (x/(1−x)^2)^r. Each fixed point of the involution must satisfy f³=f and hence f²=f, since an isotone chain map has no nontrivial cycles. Thus the nonidempotents and displaced idempotents together have even cardinality in each rank; their parities agree. Direct independent exhaustive replay of INVOLUTION_CERT.json reconstructed all maps and checked partner ranges, ranks, involution, and both inverse identities by actual composition across all 36 blocks. Counts were 1, 3, 10, 35, 126, 462, 1716, 6435. The only odd nonidempotent counts were 39 at (5,3) and 399 at (7,3), and in those two blocks the certificate moves exactly one idempotent; all other blocks move none. This attains the necessary minima, not just existence.
residual_risks: The exhaustive optimization establishes only n≤8; it does not establish a general construction or imply optimality at a larger size.

originality.rationale: Pass is for the sharp displacement classification, particularly n=6,7,8, not for the unqualified existence assertion. Distinct catalogue results cover extreme ranks, the sharp claims through five, and even mere existence through ten. The through-ten certificate is not displacement-optimal: its actual two-cycle counts force many more than the minima, including in each of n=6,7,8. The conditional rectangular-band criterion and whole-monoid permutation result do not fill that gap. Catalogue dates are not used to decide priority.
residual_risks: The broad literature lookup did not yield further pertinent results; an equivalent finite computation elsewhere remains possible. There is no priority inference from index dates.

checked_sources: Frozen RESULT.md proof and frozen matching certificate
value.rationale: Fixing idempotents where possible is a natural constraint for inverse involutions, because each can be left as its own inverse. Same-rank parity identifies a genuine obstacle, but attaining it everywhere is nontrivial; an arbitrary or larger existence certificate can move many unnecessary idempotents. The n=6–8 results give exact answers on both sides of feasibility of fixing all idempotents in a natural finite-chain family, beyond the smaller sharp cutoff and without claiming universal attainability.
residual_risks: Optimization for larger chains and a uniform construction remain open within the scope of this review.
